summary: This is the front matter and opening sections of a 2021 Forum in the European Journal of Archaeology (Volume 24, Issue 4, pp. 519-555) on populism, identity politics and the archaeology of Europe, authored by a group of twelve archaeologists led by Daniela Hofmann and Catherine J. Frieman. The introduction argues that populism threatens rational debate, that archaeological tools such as the 'culture' concept and static maps carry nationalist assumptions, and that archaeologists must change daily routines and engage wider publics. The excerpt also begins Emily Hanscam's contribution on the postnational critique of reactionary populism. Site navigation, cookie notices and author-widget markup were ignored.
one_line: Introductory forum in the European Journal of Archaeology (2021) on how populism and identity politics affect archaeology across Europe.
key_facts: The Forum 'Populism, Identity Politics, and the Archaeology of Europe' was published online by Cambridge University Press on 18 August 2021 in European Journal of Archaeology, Volume 24, Issue 4, November 2021, pp. 519-555.
The DOI of the forum is 10.1017/eaa.2021.29.

The forum has twelve listed authors, led by Daniela Hofmann and including Emily Hanscam, Martin Furholt, Martin Bača, Samantha S. Reiter, Alessandro Vanzetti, Kostas Kotsakis, Håkan Petersson, Elisabeth Niklasson, Herdis Hølleland and Catherine J. Frieman.

The introduction follows Müller (2016: 3–4) in defining 'populism' as implying exclusionary and polarizing identity politics in which difference and dissent are treated as moral failings rather than questions for compromise.
The introduction cites the then American president threatening to attack the antiquities of Iran in early 2020, described as a war crime if carried out.
The introduction notes that volumes on the Nebra Sky Disc and on archaeogenetics ended up on the German Der Spiegel non-fiction bestseller list in 2019.
The majority of the forum's texts were first presented at a session of the European Association of Archaeologists' conference in Bern in 2019.

The introduction states that the culture concept is 'widely critiqued' yet 'astonishingly persistent in large swathes of Europe', and that using 'culture' as a foundational concept risks methodological nationalism.
The introduction argues that static maps with clearly bounded coloured blobs convey unconsidered assumptions about large groups moving once from a defined origin to an end point.

The introduction describes Panich and Schneider's work on documenting Native American post-1492 persistence in parts of California, where no consistent recording exists in heritage management databases.
The introduction argues that archaeologists are 'very good at knowing what they do not want, but much worse at deciding what they want instead'.
The introduction states that university reward systems discourage public communication because it competes with writing academic papers and is not rewarded by 'publication points'.
Emily Hanscam's contribution, 'The Postnational Critique – A Response to Reactionary Populism?', states that 'Trump won the American presidency with the slogan Make America Great Again'.
Hanscam's section argues that all research concerning the past is influenced by politics and contemporary perspectives, rejecting a dualistic view of research as 'biased' or 'objective'.
